# Agent Runtime Principles {.unnumbered}

Part III developed tool, containment, and security contracts that already span jobs, leases, approvals, and uncertain effects. Part IV gives their continuing obligations a common trajectory-level owner, then develops crash persistence, effect recovery, and evaluation. The runtime carries one trajectory across its horizon, bounding the horizon exposure of H·S·A. A long horizon also reshapes the other two exposures. It turns state into a durability problem, because the evidence needed to continue must survive the process that holds it, and it turns authority into an ordering problem, because some effects cannot be undone once later steps depend on them. The part ends by measuring the single-agent system it has built, establishing the evidence needed before training or scaling it.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation .callout-principle title="Trajectory-level encapsulation"}

**Invariant**: The runtime governs each model call as part of a whole trajectory. Its runtime-owned record tracks identity, lifecycle state, actual and reserved consumption, grants and leases, continuation and live-plan references, observation eligibility, and unresolved effect obligations. The trajectory advances only through transitions and admissions that the runtime's guards permit; the model cannot write that control state directly.

**Implication**: Model output proposes changes; the runtime admits them through current state, authority, and budget checks. A late reply cannot directly update an obsolete continuation, but authenticated evidence may still be needed to settle an operation. Waiting can release a worker while cache state, workspaces, credentials, or effect obligations retain their own lifetimes. Serving-state retention remains a separate decision (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping).

:::

Owning the record gives the runtime the right to stop a trajectory. It still needs a way to know when to.

::: {#pri-vol3-preemptive-interrupts .callout-principle title="Out-of-band preemption and progress watchdogs"}

**Invariant**: A trajectory cannot be relied on to yield, to stop, or to notice that it has stopped making progress. A looping model can stay live, well formed, and inside every per-call limit while advancing nothing.

**Implication**: The runtime records control requests independently of model output and applies them through stated lifecycle guards. It can stop new admission and abort supported local work while preserving unresolved external obligations. Output quotas bound output; deadlines bound the runtime's wait. Neither proves that a remote effect has stopped. Admission accounts for actual consumption and outstanding bounded liability. Progress checks use task-scoped observations rather than heartbeats or the model's own reports. They can miss a loop or flag useful repetition; current authority and resource limits bound any intervention.

:::

A record held only in memory dies with the process that holds it.

::: {#pri-vol3-intent-before-effect .callout-principle title="Intent before effect"}

**Invariant**: The runtime preserves the decision and evidence history needed to reconstruct its selected control state under a declared failure domain. Before dispatching an external effect, it obtains the required durable acknowledgment for the authorized intent and associated admission state. The log records observations and decisions, not an omniscient account of the external world.

**Implication**: Reconstruction uses a complete surviving authoritative prefix, a compatible checkpoint, and available required artifacts under fixed update semantics. Missing intent establishes no dispatch only when complete mediation, barrier ordering, and authoritative-log completeness hold. An intent without adequate terminal outcome evidence remains unresolved; a timeout or recorded result label does not settle it. Current ownership, grants, approvals, liabilities, and endpoint repeat semantics govern further admission.

:::

The log makes the runtime's own state recoverable. The environment's state is another matter.

::: {#pri-vol3-reversibility-sagas .callout-principle title="Scoped compensation and commitment boundaries"}

**Invariant**: Recovery is defined against the state and postconditions the task requires. A snapshot can restore its selected local state under the applicable isolation and reconstruction contract; compensation is a new operation intended to establish declared application conditions. Neither erases external history, incurred charges, or unresolved effects. Irreversible commitments require an explicit policy for partial outcomes and remaining duties.

**Implication**: Before a compensable operation is dispatched, durably register its recovery template, identity, scope, dependencies, and result-binding rules. Bind endpoint-generated identities only from adequate correlated evidence. Compensations have their own admission, outcome, and repeat contracts; uncertainty or failure retains a responsible owner. A one-pivot discipline can organize a declared commitment region, respecting actual dependencies and required approval. It is not a universal limit on an entire trajectory. After commitment, preserve safe cleanup and bounded continuation or escalation rather than assuming idempotency guarantees completion.

:::

These principles organize supervision, reconstruction, and recovery for one agent. They do not establish task acceptance, and a population reliability claim cannot rest on one successful run.

::: {#pri-vol3-release-evidence .callout-principle title="Causal and statistical release evidence"}

**Invariant**: Activity signals alone do not establish task acceptance. Acceptance requires evidence for declared outcome, process, resource, and residual-duty criteria, with the coverage and limits of each check stated. Comparing system versions requires a declared task population or fixed suite, comparable trials, and uncertainty appropriate to the sampling and assignment design. Trace records connect observed decisions and outcomes without proving a unique cause.

**Implication**: Protect graders from the agent and from untrusted submitted artifacts; calibrate fallible judgments where the rubric uses them. Preserve task, configuration, candidate, operation, and attempt identities, and report capture gaps, delayed verdicts, and retention limits. Distinguish reconstruction, captured-input replay tests, and new experimental runs. A release advances under a prespecified evidence and exposure policy, while runtime authority, budgets, and unresolved-effect obligations remain in force.

:::

The four chapters of Part IV build these principles in order, each on the one before. @Sec-vol3-agent-harness gives each trajectory a record and a harness that can pause, approve, budget, and stop it without the model's cooperation, which is trajectory-level encapsulation and the preemption half of the second principle. @Sec-vol3-durable-execution specifies the recorded history, storage acknowledgment, checkpoints, and ownership needed to reconstruct selected state and admit continuation under stated failure conditions; it also distinguishes reconstruction from replay tests and new execution. @Sec-vol3-failure-recovery uses recorded evidence to choose bounded repair, compensation, containment, or escalation, governs declared commitment regions, and adds fallible task-progress checks. @Sec-vol3-evaluation then measures the single-agent system, defining the accepted task and the evidence a release requires. The runtime's enforcement contracts remain in force when the model changes; acceptance and release claims remain scoped to their checks and evidence. Part V turns to the weights. Evaluation records support subsequent curation and held-out assessment; they do not themselves certify that training on those records is safe or beneficial.
